title: Debugging, Crashes & iOS Interview Scenarios
scopeHtml: Scope: Xcode debugger, LLDB, crash logs, symbolication, common crash causes, memory warnings, interview scenario drills.

notes.title: Baseline and the debugging toolbox
notes.html:
Android equivalent. On Android you debug with Android Studio's debugger, Logcat, Layout Inspector, Profiler, and read ANR traces and Crashlytics. On iOS the equivalents are Xcode's debugger (LLDB), the console, the View Debugger, the Memory Graph, Instruments, and crash reports from Organizer or Crashlytics/Sentry.

Baseline. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials, Swift Testing. Legacy forms are shown only as "old codebase" material. Anything iOS 18/26-specific is verify.

Android iOS
Logcat Xcode console, Logger (OSLog), Console.app
Layout Inspector View Debugger (Debug View Hierarchy)
Android Profiler / Perfetto Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations, Leaks, Hangs)
LeakCanary Memory Graph Debugger, Leaks instrument
ANR trace Watchdog termination report (0x8badf00d), hang reports
Crashlytics + mapping.txt Crashlytics/Sentry + dSYM
Android Vitals Xcode Organizer, MetricKit
StrictMode Main Thread Checker, Thread Sanitizer, Address Sanitizer
adb shell xcrun simctl, devicectl, Console.app

Real industry examples. Meta, Uber and Airbnb publish hang and OOM rates per release; Sentry and Firebase Crashlytics are the two most common third-party crash reporters on iOS.

Analogy. A well-equipped garage: a stethoscope for listening (console), a lift for looking underneath (view and memory debuggers), a dynamometer for measuring (Instruments).

Common interview traps.

  • Debugging only in the simulator: memory, thermal and background behaviour differ on device.
  • Using print in production: use Logger with privacy levels.
  • Reading only Debug builds; optimizations in Release change crash shapes.

notes.title: Xcode debugger, breakpoints and LLDB commands
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Android Studio breakpoints with conditions and "Evaluate expression". Xcode uses LLDB underneath; the GUI is a thin layer, and the console (lldb) prompt is where seniors work.

Breakpoint types.

  • Line breakpoint with condition, ignore count, and actions (log a message, run a command, then automatically continue). Great for "log without recompile".
  • Symbolic breakpoint: break on a function name, for example UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints (Auto Layout conflicts) or swift_willThrow (every Swift throw).
  • Exception breakpoint: break at the point an Objective-C or Swift exception is thrown, before the stack is unwound. Add it first thing in any project.
  • Watchpoint: break when a variable's memory changes (watchpoint set variable x).
  • Runtime issue breakpoints: Main Thread Checker, Thread Sanitizer, Address Sanitizer, Undefined Behavior Sanitizer (Scheme > Diagnostics).

Core LLDB commands.

(lldb) po someObject               # print object (calls debugDescription); evaluates, can have side effects
(lldb) p count                     # print value with type
(lldb) v name                      # "frame variable": fast, no code execution, safest for Swift
(lldb) expression -l swift -- user.name = "Test"    # change state at runtime
(lldb) bt                          # backtrace of current thread
(lldb) bt all                      # all threads (find deadlocks)
(lldb) thread list
(lldb) frame select 3              # move up the stack
(lldb) frame info
(lldb) breakpoint list
(lldb) breakpoint set -n viewDidLoad
(lldb) continue / next / step / finish   # c / n / s / finish
(lldb) image lookup -a 0x104a2b1c0       # map an address to a symbol
(lldb) po Thread.isMainThread
(lldb) e -- import UIKit               # needed before touching UIKit types in some sessions
(lldb) po UIApplication.shared.keyWindow?.rootViewController   # ObjC-era trick, see note below

Swift 6 notes: LLDB runs expressions on the debugger's thread, so po on @MainActor state may show warnings; use v where possible. Expressions do not always see generic or some types; cast with as?. For SwiftUI, po self shows the view struct, not a render tree: inspect state properties instead. Debug build symbols (-Onone) allow stepping; Release builds optimize variables away ("optimized out").

Debug logging done properly.

import OSLog

private let log = Logger(subsystem: "com.example.app", category: "network")

func fetch() async {
    log.info("Fetching profile for \(userID, privacy: .private)")
    log.error("Failed: \(error.localizedDescription, privacy: .public)")
}

View logs in the Xcode console, Console.app (for a device), or log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "com.example.app"' on macOS. Signposts (OSSignposter) mark intervals for Instruments.

Real examples. Airbnb and Lyft engineering posts recommend a global exception breakpoint plus swift_willThrow for chasing hidden errors; Facebook's Chisel LLDB script collection (pviews, pvc) is an older pattern for dumping hierarchies.

Analogy. The debugger is a pause button with X-ray vision: freeze time, then ask any question about the scene.

Common interview traps.

  • Using po for everything: it runs code; prefer v for plain values.
  • Forgetting an exception breakpoint, so you land in main or UIApplicationMain with no stack.
  • Debugging Release behaviour with Debug builds, hiding optimization-dependent bugs.
  • Android mix-up: there is no adb logcat with tag filter; use Logger categories and predicates.

notes.title: View Debugger and Memory Graph
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Layout Inspector for view trees; LeakCanary for leaks. Xcode has both built in.

View Debugger (Debug > View Debugging > Capture View Hierarchy, or the toolbar icon). It exports the live view tree in 3D: you see overlapping views, clipped content, wrong frames, constraint inspector, and hidden views. For SwiftUI you see the backing UIKit hosting views and platform views, not your View structs one for one, so treat it as a rendering X-ray. In SwiftUI also use Self._printChanges() inside body to log why a view re-evaluated, and the Instruments SwiftUI template (iOS 17+, verify exact name) to see body update counts.

Memory Graph (the three-circles icon in the debug bar). It pauses the process and shows every live object with its reference edges. To hunt leaks:

  1. Enable Scheme > Diagnostics > Malloc Stack Logging (all allocation and free history) so each object shows its allocation backtrace.
  2. Reproduce the flow: open screen, close screen.
  3. Pause, open the Memory Graph, filter by your class name (for example ProfileViewModel). Any instance that should be gone is leaked.
  4. Purple "!" icons mark runtime-detected leaks. Select the object; the graph shows the retain path, and the backtrace reveals the closure or delegate holding it.

A typical retain cycle in Swift:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class ProfileViewModel {
    var onUpdate: (() -> Void)?
    func bind(to screen: ProfileScreenController) {
        onUpdate = { screen.refresh() }      // viewModel -> closure -> screen; screen -> viewModel: cycle
    }
}
// Fix
onUpdate = { [weak screen] in screen?.refresh() }
// Android: GC collects cycles, so this "just works" unless something static holds the Activity
class ProfileViewModel {
    var onUpdate: (() -> Unit)? = null
    fun bind(screen: ProfileFragment) { onUpdate = { screen.refresh() } }   // leaks only if VM outlives the Fragment
}

The ARC difference matters: Swift reference counting cannot free cycles; Kotlin's tracing GC can. Delegates should be weak var delegate: Foo? (protocol constrained to AnyObject). Unowned ([unowned self]) crashes if the target is gone, so reserve it for guaranteed lifetimes.

Real examples. Common leak sources reported across apps: NotificationCenter closure observers, Timer.scheduledTimer with a target, Combine sink capturing self, long-lived Task capturing a view model, and URLSession delegates (the session strongly retains its delegate until invalidateAndCancel). Instruments' Leaks template flags cycles; the Allocations instrument's Generations help find persistent growth.

Analogy. A leak is two people each holding the other's coat: neither can leave the cloakroom, and the coat check slowly fills up.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying [weak self] is always needed: not for non-escaping closures or short Task bodies; blanket [weak self] can hide ownership bugs.
  • Assuming SwiftUI views leak like view controllers: views are value types; leaks come from the objects they own (@State models, closures).
  • Forgetting to invalidate Timer/URLSession/KVO.
  • Android mix-up: LeakCanary finds GC-reachable leaks; ARC leaks are about cycles, a different class of bug.

notes.title: Reading crash reports
notes.html:
Android equivalent. A Java stack trace plus mapping.txt deobfuscation; ANR traces from /data/anr. An iOS crash report (.ips/.crash) is a text/JSON file that lists the crashed thread, an exception type, and a binary-image list; it is symbolicated using dSYMs.

Anatomy of a report (abridged):

Incident Identifier: 8E3A...-...
Hardware Model:      iPhone15,2
OS Version:          iPhone OS 17.5 (21F79)
Exception Type:      EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)
Exception Subtype:   KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000010
Termination Reason:  SIGNAL 11 Segmentation fault: 11
Triggered by Thread: 0

Thread 0 name:  Dispatch queue: com.apple.main-thread
Thread 0 Crashed:
0   MyApp    0x0000000104a2b1c0 ProfileViewModel.name.getter + 40
1   MyApp    0x0000000104a1c398 closure #1 in ProfileView.body.getter + 120
2   SwiftUI  0x00000001d4f3a2c4 ...

How to read it.

  1. Exception Type tells the category:
    • EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV/SIGBUS): invalid memory access. In Swift it usually comes from unsafe code, an over-released Objective-C object, unowned access to a dead object, a data race corrupting memory, or deep stack recursion (stack overflow shows as KERN_PROTECTION_FAILURE on the guard page).
    • EXC_BREAKPOINT (SIGTRAP): a Swift runtime trap: force-unwrapping nil, Array index out of range, integer overflow, failed precondition/fatalError, try!. The most common Swift crash.
    • EXC_CRASH (SIGABRT): abort, typically an uncaught Objective-C exception (NSInvalidArgumentException, "unrecognized selector", UIKit main-thread violation, Auto Layout). The "Last Exception Backtrace" and "Application Specific Information" hold the message.
    • EXC_BAD_INSTRUCTION: older Swift trap signal for the same class as EXC_BREAKPOINT on Intel.
    • EXC_RESOURCE: CPU or memory limit violations (reports include wakeups or memory limits).
  2. Termination Reason / code. 0x8badf00d ("ate food") = watchdog killed a slow app, 0xdead10cc = suspended while holding a file lock or database (SQLite in a shared App Group container), 0xc00010ff = thermal, 0xbaadca11 = failed to respond to a PushKit/CallKit report, 0xdeadfa11 = force quit while unresponsive. Exact list: verify in Apple's "Understanding the exception types in a crash report".
  3. Thread 0 vs others: main thread crash vs background; look at the crashed thread's top frames in your module.
  4. Binary Images: the UUID of your binary must match a dSYM UUID.

Key Swift crash messages (appear in Application Specific Information / console, not always in the report):

  • Fatal error: Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value
  • Fatal error: Index out of range
  • Thread 1: Fatal error: Range requires lowerBound <= upperBound
  • Swift runtime failure: arithmetic overflow
  • Simultaneous accesses to 0x..., but modification requires exclusive access (exclusivity enforcement)
  • Swift 6 / concurrency: Incorrect actor executor assumption (dispatch_assert_queue_fail) when @MainActor code runs off the main thread, via an unsafe assumeIsolated.

Where reports come from: Xcode Organizer > Crashes (App Store users who opted in to share diagnostics), TestFlight feedback, Window > Devices and Simulators > View Device Logs, and SDKs (Crashlytics, Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog). MetricKit's MXDiagnosticPayload delivers crash and hang diagnostics to the app itself (iOS 14+ for payloads, crashes iOS 15+, verify).

Real examples. Teams at Spotify and Duolingo triage by crash-free sessions percentage and by top signature; teams keep Organizer, Crashlytics and Sentry side by side because their sampling differs.

Analogy. A crash report is a police incident report: type of incident (exception), where it happened (thread), the witness list (binary images), and the physical evidence (backtrace) that only makes sense with a map (dSYM).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing EXC_BREAKPOINT (a Swift trap, deterministic) with EXC_BAD_ACCESS (memory corruption, often nondeterministic).
  • Reading an unsymbolicated report and blaming the last visible Apple frame.
  • Ignoring Termination Reason; the code usually names the cause.
  • Android mix-up: there is no ANR dialog; the OS silently kills the app and writes a watchdog report.

notes.title: Symbolication with dSYMs
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Upload mapping.txt to Play Console / Crashlytics so R8-obfuscated stack traces become readable. On iOS, the compiled binary keeps only addresses; the dSYM bundle holds symbol names, file and line info keyed by the build's UUID.

Crash (address 0x104a2b1c0 in MyApp)
        |  match UUID of "MyApp" binary image  <->  UUID inside MyApp.app.dSYM
        v
ProfileViewModel.swift:42  ProfileViewModel.name.getter

Workflow.

  • Build setting Debug Information Format = DWARF with dSYM File for Release (the default for Archive). Archives in the Organizer include the dSYMs.
  • For Apple-delivered builds via App Store Connect with bitcode removed (bitcode is deprecated since Xcode 14), the dSYMs generated at your archive time are the right ones. If you used bitcode in an older build, App Store Connect re-compiled and you must download dSYMs from App Store Connect (verify for legacy builds).
  • Upload dSYMs to your crash service via a Run Script build phase (Crashlytics upload-symbols, Sentry CLI sentry-cli debug-files upload) or in CI (Fastlane upload_symbols_to_crashlytics).
  • Local symbolication: Xcode symbolicates automatically when you drag a .crash/.ips into Devices and Simulators > View Device Logs, or use the command line.
# find the UUID of your binary and your dSYM; they must match
dwarfdump --uuid MyApp.app.dSYM
dwarfdump --uuid MyApp.app/MyApp

# symbolicate a single address (load address from the Binary Images section)
xcrun atos -arch arm64 -o MyApp.app.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/MyApp \
     -l 0x104a00000 0x104a2b1c0

# Spotlight search for a dSYM by UUID
mdfind "com_apple_xcode_dsym_uuids == 8E3A1C4D-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"

Failure modes. Missing dSYM (Crashlytics shows "Missing dSYM" warnings), wrong dSYM (every rebuild changes the UUID unless the build is reproducible), SPM binary frameworks and third-party XCFrameworks need their own dSYMs, and stripped symbols in Release (Strip Linked Product) are normal and expected when dSYMs are archived. Keep dSYMs for every released version, forever, in CI artefacts.

Real examples. An outage story often retold: a team shipped a hotfix built on a different CI machine and the dSYM did not match, so a week of crashes was unreadable. Fix: archive and upload dSYMs from the same pipeline that builds the IPA.

Analogy. Without the dSYM the crash report is a ransom note made of street coordinates; the dSYM is the address book that turns them into names.

Common interview traps.

  • Re-building to "regenerate" the dSYM: a rebuild produces a new UUID and does not match the shipped binary.
  • Forgetting dSYMs for embedded frameworks.
  • Android mix-up: a lost mapping.txt is the same sin, but iOS reports also carry line numbers only if the dSYM has them.

notes.title: Common crash causes and their fixes
notes.html:
Android equivalent. NPE (!!), IndexOutOfBounds, NetworkOnMainThread/CalledFromWrongThread, leaked Activities, OOM. Swift's compiler removes many null bugs, yet a handful of patterns still cause most iOS crashes.

1. Force unwrap and try!. Compile-time safe, runtime fatal.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Crash: EXC_BREAKPOINT "Unexpectedly found nil"
let name = user.profile!.name
let url = URL(string: input)!               // user-provided string
let model = try! JSONDecoder().decode(Model.self, from: data)

// Safe
guard let name = user.profile?.name else { return }
guard let url = URL(string: input) else { throw InputError.badURL }
let model = try JSONDecoder().decode(Model.self, from: data)
val name = user.profile!!.name                         // NullPointerException
val name2 = user.profile?.name ?: return               // safe

2. Index out of range. array[i] traps; there is no getOrNull. Add a safe subscript extension or use .first, .indices.contains(i). Typical cause: stale index after a mutation in ForEach/table updates, data source and numberOfRows out of sync (NSInternalInconsistencyException in UIKit batch updates).

3. Main-thread violations. UIKit and SwiftUI state must change on the main actor. Symptoms: purple runtime warning "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed" (SwiftUI), "UIKit should only be used from the main thread" (Main Thread Checker), or random crashes in layout. Fix with @MainActor on view models and await MainActor.run {} only at boundaries. Swift 6 strict concurrency turns many of these into compile errors.

4. Retain cycles and over-retention. Gradual memory growth, then jetsam; see the Memory Graph section.

5. Unrecognized selector / KVC (Objective-C interop). -[NSNull length]: unrecognized selector, an @objc method renamed, or an @IBOutlet missing after a rename: this class is not key value coding-compliant for the key .... Fix by removing stale outlets in the storyboard/xib.

6. Concurrency and exclusivity. Data races in legacy GCD code (corrupted arrays, EXC_BAD_ACCESS), "Simultaneous accesses" exclusivity violations, deadlocks from DispatchQueue.main.sync while already on main (a hang, not a crash), and misuse of withCheckedContinuation (resuming twice is a runtime error, never resuming leaks the task). Use actors and Sendable; enable Thread Sanitizer in test schemes.

7. Decoding and data. DecodingError.keyNotFound or typeMismatch thrown on server changes; try! turns it into a crash. SwiftData/Core Data faults on a deleted object, migration failure at launch (the app crashes on every launch: the worst kind), NSManagedObject used on the wrong context (EXC_BAD_ACCESS/"threading violation").

8. Missing Info.plist keys / entitlements. Accessing camera, location, photos, Face ID (NSFaceIDUsageDescription) without the usage string aborts the app.

9. Stack overflow. Infinite recursion (a computed property calling itself, accidental didSet loop) gives EXC_BAD_ACCESS with a long repeating stack.

10. Third-party SDK and OS version issues. Use of an API not available on the deployment target: @available and #available guards; crashes only on older OS versions appear in Organizer filtered by OS.

Real examples. The Swift forums are full of "migrated to Swift 6 and found a hundred latent data races"; large apps routinely discover that most of their top-10 crashes are try!/! or invalid UIKit updates from callbacks.

Analogy. Crashes are the same few road hazards repeatedly: potholes (nil), missing guardrails (index), wrong-lane driving (threads), and slowly leaking tyres (memory).

Common interview traps.

  • "Swift has no null crashes": force unwrap and implicitly unwrapped optionals (var x: Foo!) bring them back.
  • Wrapping a crash in DispatchQueue.main.async as a "fix" without finding the root cause.
  • Ignoring that a crash on launch after a data migration means every user is stuck; ship migrations behind tested paths.

notes.title: Memory warnings, jetsam and the watchdog
notes.html:
Android equivalent. onTrimMemory(level) callbacks, the low-memory killer (LMK/lmkd) and per-app heap limits that throw OutOfMemoryError; ANR after about 5 seconds of main thread block. iOS has no swap, and both memory and responsiveness are enforced by the OS killing your process.

Jetsam (memory). When the device is under memory pressure, the kernel's jetsam daemon kills processes by priority: background and suspended apps first, the foreground app last, but the foreground app is killed if it exceeds its per-process limit. There is no OutOfMemoryError: the app simply disappears, and the report is a JetsamEvent log (not a normal crash), EXC_RESOURCE, or only an Organizer "Memory" termination entry. Limits depend on device RAM and are not published as fixed numbers (rough guidance is on the order of 1 to 3 GB for the foreground app on recent iPhones; verify, do not quote as exact). The entitlement com.apple.developer.kernel.increased-memory-limit exists for apps that need more (verify).

Warnings. UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification and UIViewController.didReceiveMemoryWarning() are polite last chances: drop image caches, release large buffers. NSCache evicts automatically under pressure (unlike Dictionary).

NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
    forName: UIApplication.didReceiveMemoryWarningNotification,
    object: nil, queue: .main) { _ in
    ImageCache.shared.removeAll()
}

How to find the cause. Xcode debug navigator Memory gauge; Instruments Allocations (generations, persistent bytes, "Mark Generation" before and after a flow), VM Tracker (dirty memory), and the Memory Graph. Frequent culprits: full-size image decoding (a 12 MP photo decodes to about 48 MB: width × height × 4 bytes; downsample with CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex), unbounded caches, large arrays loaded from SwiftData without fetch limits, video frames, and leaked view models. Clean up with autoreleasepool {} inside tight Objective-C-bridged loops.

Watchdog (responsiveness). The system kills an app that does not complete launch or a lifecycle transition in time, and the report carries 0x8badf00d. Launch timeouts are roughly 20 seconds in the classic description (verify; the exact value varies by phase). Typical causes: synchronous network calls or database migrations on the main thread at launch, DispatchQueue.main.sync deadlocks, waiting on a semaphore on the main thread, or heavy didFinishLaunching work. Smaller freezes, a hang (main thread blocked above roughly 250 ms by Apple's definition, "hitch" for short dropped frames), appear in Organizer's "Hang rate" and Instruments' Hangs and Animation Hitches templates; MetricKit's MXHangDiagnostic collects them in the field.

// Fix pattern: defer heavy launch work; keep main thread free
@main struct MyApp: App {
    init() { /* only essentials */ }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { RootView().task { await Warmup.run() } }   // async, off main when possible
    }
}

Also relevant: background task expiry (beginBackgroundTask must be ended before time runs out, otherwise 0x8badf00d while backgrounded), and thermal state (ProcessInfo.thermalState) throttling.

Real examples. Facebook's well-known "OOM" work (iOS "FOOM") tracked unexplained foreground terminations by elimination (no crash, no exit, not a user kill); Uber and Pinterest document image downsampling after OOM spikes.

Analogy. Jetsam is a nightclub bouncer: when the room is overcrowded, whoever has been standing in the back longest leaves first, and if you keep bringing guests (memory) you get thrown out too. The watchdog is the bar closing at midnight regardless of whether you are in the middle of your drink.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a catchable error for memory exhaustion: there is none.
  • Treating didReceiveMemoryWarning as guaranteed; many jetsam kills come with no warning.
  • Quoting an exact RAM limit as fact.
  • Blocking launch with a database migration; do it behind a progress UI or in a background task.

notes.title: Scenario drills
notes.html:
Android equivalent. These are the same system-design/debug questions you know from Android interviews, with the iOS vocabulary swapped in. Practice answering each in this order: clarify, measure, locate, fix, prevent.

Drill 1: slow list. "A feed with images stutters while scrolling."

  1. Measure: Instruments Animation Hitches and Time Profiler; Xcode Organizer scroll hitch rate. Separate main thread work from rendering (GPU) work (Core Animation instrument, offscreen rendering, blending).
  2. Typical causes: image decode on main, huge images, heavy body computation, unstable ForEach identity (use Identifiable with stable ids, not \.self on changing values, not array index), expensive formatters created per cell (DateFormatter is costly), AnyView type erasure breaking diffing, List row view re-evaluated due to a broad @Observable dependency.
  3. Fixes: LazyVStack/List for lazy loading; downsample and cache images (Nuke, Kingfisher, AsyncImage has weak caching); precompute row models; move work off main using async/Task.detached; paginate; use .drawingGroup() sparingly; use Equatable views and smaller subviews. UIKit: diffable data source, prefetchDataSource, reuse identifiers, avoid autolayout recursion in cells.
  4. Prevent: hitch metrics in CI via XCTMetric (XCTOSSignpostMetric/XCTHitchMetric, verify), performance tests.

Drill 2: leaky screen. "Memory climbs each time the user opens and closes the order screen."

  1. Reproduce with the Allocations generations or the Memory Graph (Malloc Stack Logging on).
  2. Find the retained view model or controller; follow the reference chain to the culprit: closure capture, timer, NotificationCenter block observer, Combine AnyCancellable stored in a long-lived singleton, Task loop that never cancels, delegate strongly held.
  3. Fix with [weak self], weak var delegate, cancelling tasks in .task (automatic cancellation on view disappearance), invalidating timers in deinit (log in deinit to prove release).
  4. Prevent: a unit test asserting a weak reference becomes nil after dismissal; unit tests with a leak checker helper.
@Test @MainActor func viewModelDeallocates() async {
    weak var weakVM: OrderViewModel?
    do {
        let vm = OrderViewModel(service: .mock)
        weakVM = vm
        await vm.load()
    }
    #expect(weakVM == nil)       // verify in your Swift Testing version: lifetime semantics under optimization
}

Drill 3: flaky login. "Some users get logged out randomly or cannot log in on iOS only." Checklist: token refresh race (multiple 401s trigger parallel refreshes: serialize with an actor so only one refresh runs, others await it), Keychain accessibility class (kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked fails when a background fetch runs on a locked device: use AfterFirstUnlock), Keychain data surviving app reinstall (treat first launch separately), clock skew on JWT expiry, URLSession cookie storage differences, Sign in with Apple private relay email mismatches and missing first-login name, app launched in the background by a push (no UI session yet), Universal Link callback arriving before the app is ready (cold start queue), iCloud Keychain restore on a new device.

actor TokenStore {
    private var refreshTask: Task<Token, Error>?
    func validToken() async throws -> Token {
        if let existing = refreshTask { return try await existing.value }
        let task = Task { try await AuthAPI.refresh() }
        refreshTask = task
        defer { refreshTask = nil }
        return try await task.value
    }
}

Drill 4: offline-first design. "Design a notes app that works offline and syncs."

  • Single source of truth: local store (SwiftData/Core Data/SQLite via GRDB); UI observes it (@Query); network updates the store, never the UI directly. Same as Room + Flow.
  • Write path: user edits write locally and enqueue an operation in an outbox (id, type, payload, retry count, client timestamp). A sync engine drains the outbox when NWPathMonitor reports connectivity, with exponential backoff; use background URLSession and BGAppRefreshTask/BGProcessingTask for opportunistic sync, and silent push to trigger pulls (not guaranteed).
  • Conflicts: last-write-wins with server versions, per-field merge, or CRDTs for collaborative text. Use stable client-generated UUIDs for create idempotency and an idempotency key header.
  • Pagination cursors, tombstones for deletes, schema migration plan, encryption at rest (data protection class), and observability (sync status, error banners).
  • iOS specifics: the app may be suspended mid-sync, so operations must be resumable; background execution time is limited; CloudKit with SwiftData offers built-in sync for Apple-only products (verify model restrictions: no unique constraints, optional relationships).

Real examples. Notion, Bear, Things and WhatsApp follow local-first outbox designs; Linear's sync engine is a well-known web/mobile local-first example.

Analogy. Drills are fire drills: the building will not burn, but the people who practiced the exits move quickly when it does.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to a fix before measuring.
  • Saying "use weak self everywhere" for leaks.
  • Offline design that updates the UI from the network directly instead of a local source of truth.
  • Assuming background sync always runs: iOS decides when.

notes.title: Talking about iOS in an interview as an Android specialist
notes.html:
Android equivalent. You would answer "tell me about your experience" with projects and depth. Here the pattern is: lead with transferable depth, be explicit about your iOS exposure, show a learning trajectory with evidence.

A structure that works.

  1. Position: "Three years of production Android (Kotlin, Compose, coroutines/Flow, Hilt, Room). Over the last N weeks I built X in Swift/SwiftUI, shipped Y to TestFlight."
  2. Map, do not equate: "In Android I handled this with ViewModel and StateFlow; in iOS I would use an @Observable model on the main actor, and the key difference is value semantics and ARC."
  3. Name the unfamiliar honestly: "I have not shipped an app through App Store review; I know the flow from TestFlight, signing, and privacy manifests, and here is what I would check first."
  4. Show the debugging depth: you can read a crash report, symbolicate it, use the Memory Graph, and reason about main-thread hangs. That is what separates tourists from engineers.
  5. Show product thinking: platform conventions, accessibility, and release cadence.

Sample answers.

  • "Why did you get a retain-cycle leak when Android has none?" "Android's GC is tracing so cycles are collected; ARC counts references, so a closure capturing self that self stores is a cycle. I use [weak self] for escaping closures stored on long-lived objects and check with the Memory Graph."
  • "How do you keep iOS and Android in sync?" "A contract-first API with generated models, tolerant decoding of unknown enum values, feature flags, shared analytics schema, and a parity matrix."
  • "How would you share code?" "KMP for the domain and data layers with SKIE, native UI; I would not use Compose Multiplatform for a design-led consumer app unless the team can invest in platform polish."
  • "What is a thing you got wrong in iOS?" Have one real story: forgot NSCameraUsageDescription and crashed, blocked the main thread in init, or mis-handled optional unwrapping.

Prepare a portfolio. A small public SwiftUI app with SwiftData persistence, async networking, Swift Testing unit tests, a widget, and a README that explains architecture choices; notes on a retain cycle you found and fixed; a symbolicated crash walkthrough.

What interviewers probe. Swift value vs reference semantics, @State vs @Binding vs @Observable ownership, structured concurrency and actor isolation, ARC and closures, the app lifecycle and scene phases, Core Data or SwiftData concurrency, testing with protocols, Instruments literacy, App Store process.

Analogy. A seasoned cook joining a new cuisine: you are hired for your knife skills and judgment; you earn trust by saying "I don't know this spice yet" and then tasting carefully.

Common interview traps.

  • Bluffing about App Store submission experience.
  • Pretending equivalence ("a ViewController is just an Activity") without naming differences.
  • Offering only Android stories to every iOS question; connect them back to the iOS mechanism.
  • Dismissing UIKit and Objective-C; many codebases still depend on them.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Debugging toolbox: LLDB (v, po, bt, expression), exception and symbolic breakpoints, Main Thread Checker and sanitizers, View Debugger, Memory Graph with Malloc Stack Logging.
  • ARC leaks come from cycles (closures, delegates, timers, observers); GC-based Android intuition hides them, so use [weak self] thoughtfully and verify with Memory Graph.
  • Crash reports: read Exception Type (EXC_BREAKPOINT Swift trap, EXC_BAD_ACCESS memory, SIGABRT uncaught exception), Termination Reason (0x8badf00d watchdog), and crashed thread; symbolicate with the matching dSYM (UUID must match).
  • Top crash causes: force unwrap, index out of range, main-thread UI updates, data races, bad decoding, missing Info.plist keys, migrations.
  • iOS kills for memory (jetsam, no catchable error) and for slowness (watchdog); downsample images, bound caches, keep launch light.
  • Scenario drills follow clarify, measure, locate, fix, prevent; offline-first means a local source of truth plus an outbox and resilient sync.
  • In interviews, lead with transferable depth, map concepts without equating them, and be honest about gaps while showing evidence of iOS work.
